cards.definitions: For m,n≥1, a map f:{0,1}ᵐ→{0,1}ⁿ is d-local if each output coordinate depends on at most d input coordinates; the chosen inputs may differ between outputs and may be shared. The input Uₘ is uniform on {0,1}ᵐ, and X is the law of f(Uₘ). There is no bound on m and no algorithmic uniformity requirement across n. For nonempty S⊆{0,…,n}, let U_Sⁿ be uniform on all strings x∈{0,1}ⁿ with |x|=Σⱼxⱼ∈S: every such string, rather than every allowed weight, has the same probability. For distributions P,Q on {0,1}ⁿ, TV(P,Q)=½Σₓ|P(x)−Q(x)|. The six comparison distributions are: a point mass at 0ⁿ; a point mass at 1ⁿ; equal mass on 0ⁿ and 1ⁿ; uniform on all even-weight strings; uniform on all odd-weight strings; and uniform on the entire cube. The quantifiers in the historical claim are ∃C>0 ∀d≥0 ∀ε∈(0,1) ∃n₀(d,ε) ∀n≥n₀ ∀m≥1 ∀d-local f ∀nonempty S: TV(f(Uₘ),U_Sⁿ)≤ε implies min_D TV(f(Uₘ),D)≤Cε, where D ranges over those six distributions. The result actually allows the threshold n₀ to depend only on d. No symmetry of f or of its output distribution is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative resolution is Theorem 4.1 of Kane, Ostuni and Wu, which proves the stated robust six-distribution classification, with an absolute multiplicative constant. cards.definitions: Graphs are finite undirected loopless multigraphs, allowing parallel edges as in the source’s expanding-expander setting; each edge copy contributes one to each endpoint’s degree. A graph is d-regular when every vertex has degree d. Its symmetric adjacency matrix counts edge multiplicities and has real eigenvalues λ₁=d≥λ₂≥⋯≥λₙ. Here the Ramanujan condition bounds all eigenvalues except the top one, including the bottom eigenvalue in absolute value. In particular these graphs are connected and nonbipartite. For n∈I, let n⁺ be the least element of I larger than n. Compare Gₙ and Gₙ⁺ on their shared labels, adjoining the new labels as isolated vertices before inserting or deleting edges. The edit cost is Σ_{1≤u<v≤n⁺}|aₙ(u,v)−aₙ⁺(u,v)|, with aₙ(u,v)=0 if an endpoint exceeds n. The constant c is independent of n and may depend on the chosen fixed degree. New vertices remain in later graphs. Bounded cost also forces bounded gaps between consecutive sizes. The question asks for existence; no efficient construction, prescribed degree, exact cost such as 3d, or every-integer size set is imposed. The separate bipartite variant in the source excludes both trivial eigenvalues ±d and is not the condition displayed here.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the existence of one such infinite family with fixed d≥3 and uniformly bounded edit cost, or rule out every such family. A construction may be nonexplicit. cards.definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A minor is obtained by deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, with loops removed and parallel edges suppressed. An H-minor model in G consists of pairwise disjoint connected vertex sets B_v for v∈V(H), with an edge between B_u and B_v for each uv∈E(H); its support is their union. Let pack_H(G) be the largest number of models with mutually disjoint supports, and let τ_H(G) be the minimum number of vertices whose deletion leaves no H minor. The integral Erdős–Pósa property on C means that a function f:N_0→N_0 exists such that τ_H(G)≤f(pack_H(G)) for every G∈C. This one f may depend on H and C, but not on the individual graph. A class is minor-closed if it contains every minor of each of its graphs. A graph parameter is invariant under graph isomorphism and is minor-monotone when G′ a minor of G implies p_H(G′)≤p_H(G). Boundedness on C means one finite bound for all graphs in C. H need not be connected. No efficient evaluation algorithm or uniquely prescribed parameter is part of the conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative answer follows from the published finite obstruction-sequence characterization: for the target class of H-minor-free graphs, take p_H(G) to be the largest order of an obstruction in its fixed finite collection of increasing minor sequences that occurs as a minor of G, using 0 when none occurs. Minor monotonicity and the theorem’s excluded-sequence criterion give exactly the required equivalence.

context_blocks.title: Packing and deletion measure the same obstruction differently
context_blocks.text: Packing asks for many vertex-disjoint occurrences of H as a minor. Covering asks for a small common vertex set meeting every such occurrence. An Erdős–Pósa function says that bounded packing forces bounded covering throughout a whole graph class.

context_blocks.title: The parameter must precede the environment class
context_blocks.text: Choosing a separate arbitrary parameter after seeing C would weaken the conjecture. Here H alone determines p_H, and boundedness of that one parameter recognizes every minor-closed class where the duality holds.

context_blocks.title: The later theorem supplies the missing characterization
context_blocks.text: Paul, Protopapas, Thilikos and Wiederrecht give a finite collection of obstruction sequences for every proper minor-closed target class. A minor-closed environment has integral packing–covering duality precisely when it excludes some member of every sequence. Applying this to H-minor-free target graphs yields the conjectured parameter.

context_blocks.title: Integral and half-integral packing are different
context_blocks.text: Half-integral packing allows each vertex to belong to two chosen models. The source paper’s half-integral results alone do not settle this card. The later theorem characterizes the integral duality required here. For planar H, the classical integral theorem already holds on all graphs, so the constant parameter p_H=0 suffices.

cards.definitions: A graph is finite, undirected and simple. A graph class C transduces all graphs if there is one first-order formula φ(x,y), using adjacency, equality and a fixed finite list of unary vertex predicates, with this property: every finite graph H can be obtained by choosing G∈C, assigning arbitrary subsets of V(G) to those predicates, joining distinct vertices u,v whenever φ(u,v) or φ(v,u) holds in that colored G, and taking an induced subgraph isomorphic to H. First-order quantifiers range over vertices; φ and its predicate list must be fixed independently of H, while G and its coloring may vary. C is monadically NIP, also called monadically dependent, if no such φ exists. A k-flip of G partitions V(G) into at most k parts and independently complements or retains adjacency between each unordered pair of parts, permitting a pair to consist of the same part; loops are never added. The resulting graph has the same vertices. C is flip-breakable if, for every integer radius r≥0, there exist an integer kᵣ and a function Nᵣ:ℕ₊→ℕ₊ such that for every m≥1, every G∈C and every W⊆V(G) with |W|≥Nᵣ(m), there exist A,B⊆W with |A|,|B|≥m and a kᵣ-flip H of G for which dist_H(A,B)>r. Here dist_H(A,B) is the minimum shortest-path distance between one vertex of A and one of B, with distance infinity across components. The constants depend on C and r, not on G,W or m. No hereditary-closure assumption is required for this equivalence.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative answer is the published flip-breakability equivalence of Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk, Theorem 1.3 in the full version. Its two directions exactly characterize all monadically NIP graph classes by a condition involving only graph partitions, adjacency changes, subsets and distances.

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class C of finite simple graphs, do there exist a deterministic algorithm A_C, a computable function f_C:N→N and a constant d_C such that A_C decides whether G satisfies a first-order sentence φ in time f_C(|φ|)(|V(G)|+1)^{d_C} for every G∈C? The precise effectiveness condition is given below; the graph is supplied without a structural decomposition.
cards.definitions: The class C is fixed, is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs, and is not part of each input. First-order sentences use equality, adjacency E(x,y), Boolean connectives and quantifiers over individual vertices. They do not quantify over sets, and no vertex order or arithmetic is supplied. The input is the explicitly represented graph G and the sentence φ; the parameter k=|φ| is its encoded length. The algorithm must halt on every input, and its correctness and stated time bound are required when G∈C; it need not recognize membership in C. To define monadic dependence, let θ(x,y) be any fixed first-order formula using adjacency and finitely many additional unary predicates. A graph in T_θ(G) is obtained by interpreting these predicates as arbitrary vertex subsets, putting an edge between distinct u,v whenever θ(u,v) or θ(v,u) holds, and taking any induced subgraph. C is monadically dependent when no single θ gives all finite graphs among the outputs T_θ(G), G∈C. For an explicit effective version, define P_s as the bipartite powerset graph with vertices a₁,…,a_s and b_S for every S⊆{1,…,s}, and edges a_i b_S exactly when i∈S. Require a computable function b:N→N_{≥1} such that, for every formula θ and every G∈C, P_{b(|θ|)} is absent from T_θ(G). Formula length includes its predicate symbols under a fixed effective encoding. This is the computable dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24. The programs computing b and the eventual algorithm may depend on C; they are not extra per-instance certificates. The exponent d_C is independent of k. The query-evaluation problem here is for the plain graph signature; unary colours occur in the structural definition. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether excluding arbitrary first-order graph encoding exactly supplies the structure needed for tractable logical queries on hereditary graph classes.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper. The independent-side hardness and stable-side algorithm are known; radius-one merge-width does not provide the full algorithm. This card fixes the effective dependence-function convention to require a computable FPT bound. No resolution found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: First-order logic describes many small graph queries with quantifiers over vertices. For example, the existence of a dominating set of size k can be expressed by choosing k vertices and requiring every vertex to equal or be adjacent to one of them. A direct evaluation can try n^k choices. Fixed-parameter tractability asks for the stronger form f(k)n^d: the query may be expensive, but its length must not keep increasing the exponent of the graph size.

Graph structure can make this possible. The broad research programme asks which hereditary classes support such evaluation. Hereditary means that deleting vertices keeps a graph inside the class, a natural closure property when a query examines a portion of a database or network. Sparse graph classes gave early positive results, but dense classes with controlled structure also admit efficient model checking. Thus density alone cannot describe the boundary.

Monadic dependence measures whether unrestricted graph structure can be hidden inside a class through a fixed logical interpretation. Unary predicates mark arbitrary vertex subsets. A formula then defines new edges, after which selected vertices may be retained. If this process can generate every finite graph, apparently restricted inputs still contain arbitrary graph complexity in an interpretable form. Monadic dependence forbids that possibility.

The effective hypothesis matters to the exact computational claim. A structural class can have finite obstruction bounds at every logical complexity while those bounds grow faster than any computable function. Mählmann makes the dependence condition quantitative using forbidden powerset graphs and distinguishes computable parameter bounds from weaker conventions for fixed-parameter tractability. This card adopts that explicit effective formulation, so “there exists a finite bound” is not silently substituted for an algorithmically bounded parameter function.

One direction of the broader classification has been established. Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that first-order model checking is AW[*]-hard on every hereditary monadically independent graph class. Under the standard assumption FPT≠AW[*], this excludes efficient model checking on the independent side. Their structural characterization uses flip-breakability, a separation property allowing controlled changes to adjacency between vertex groups. The missing direction is the algorithm for dependent classes.

A major positive theorem proves fixed-parameter tractability for monadically stable classes. Stability additionally forbids interpreting arbitrarily long linear orders; dependence forbids arbitrary graph encoding and allows more classes. The 2023 preprint by Dreier, Eleftheriadis, Mählmann, McCarty, Pilipczuk and Toruńczyk, published at FOCS 2024, settles the stable case using neighborhood complexity and suitable covers. It does not make the two structural notions equivalent.

Merge-width is a graph parameter used in existing model-checking theorems. Dreier and Toruńczyk describe a graph by a sequence of successively coarser vertex partitions, recording deviations from default adjacencies between parts. Their model-checking theorem applies to bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. This theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied and does not cover the stated input model.

The July 2026 neighborhood-complexity paper proves that, for every fixed positive η, the number of distinct sets N(v)∩A is O(|A|^{1+η}) in a monadically dependent class, with the constant depending on the class and η. It also constructs sequences witnessing radius-one merge-width n^{o(1)} in polynomial time. This supplies a concrete structural and algorithmic step. General first-order formulas require control at radii depending on the formula, so radius one does not complete the model-checking argument.

Related February 2026 work by Dreier and Kuske accelerates the construction of low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, improving model-checking runtimes within the already tractable monadically stable setting. Such refinements are useful because they make the structural tools more practical, while leaving the dependent-versus-stable boundary in place.

A positive answer would unify several major algorithmic graph frameworks through one logical condition and explain when small declarative queries can avoid repeated high-dimensional enumeration. A counterexample satisfying the effective hypothesis would show that the absence of arbitrary logical graph encoding is insufficient for tractability. Either outcome would sharpen the connection between graph structure and query evaluation.

Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
